lessons.title: IBM Qiskit Developer Certification Overview
lessons.content:
IBM Qiskit Developer Certification Overview

🎓 Your Path to Certification

The IBM Certified Associate Developer - Quantum Computation using Qiskit certification validates your ability to use Qiskit to build, execute, and optimize quantum circuits.

Exam Details

Exam Code C1000-112
Number of Questions 60 multiple choice
Time Limit 90 minutes
Passing Score ~70% (42/60)
Format Online proctored
Cost $200 USD

Exam Topics & Weights

Quantum Circuits ~25%

Gates, measurements, circuit construction

Operators & States ~20%

Statevector, operators, quantum info

Transpilation ~15%

Optimization levels, basis gates, coupling maps

Running on Backends ~20%

Simulators, real hardware, primitives

Visualization & Tools ~20%

Circuit drawing, histograms, state visualization

Study Resources

Qiskit Textbook

learning.quantum.ibm.com

Qiskit Documentation

docs.quantum.ibm.com

IBM Quantum Learning

Courses and tutorials from IBM

This Course!

Practice exams and topic reviews

Exam Tips

  • Know the Qiskit API well - method names, parameters
  • Practice reading circuits and predicting outputs
  • Understand transpilation options and effects
  • Be comfortable with state vectors and operators
  • Know the difference between Sampler and Estimator
keyTakeaways: Focus areas: circuits, operators, transpilation, backends

lessons.title: Quantum Circuit Fundamentals Review
lessons.content:
Quantum Circuit Fundamentals Review

📚 Key Exam Topic: ~25%

This section reviews the circuit concepts most commonly tested on the certification exam.

Circuit Creation

# Key constructors - KNOW THESE!
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, QuantumRegister, ClassicalRegister

# Method 1: Simple
qc = QuantumCircuit(3)  # 3 qubits, no classical bits
qc = QuantumCircuit(3, 3)  # 3 qubits, 3 classical bits

# Method 2: With registers
qr = QuantumRegister(2, 'q')
cr = ClassicalRegister(2, 'c')
qc = QuantumCircuit(qr, cr)

# Properties you should know:
print(qc.num_qubits)     # Number of qubits
print(qc.num_clbits)     # Number of classical bits
print(qc.depth())        # Circuit depth
print(qc.width())        # Total width (qubits + clbits)
print(qc.size())         # Number of operations

Essential Gates

Single-Qubit Gates

qc.x(0)     # Pauli-X (NOT)
qc.y(0)     # Pauli-Y
qc.z(0)     # Pauli-Z
qc.h(0)     # Hadamard
qc.s(0)     # S gate (√Z)
qc.t(0)     # T gate (√S)
qc.rx(θ, 0) # Rotation X
qc.ry(θ, 0) # Rotation Y
qc.rz(θ, 0) # Rotation Z

Multi-Qubit Gates

qc.cx(0, 1)   # CNOT
qc.cy(0, 1)   # CY
qc.cz(0, 1)   # CZ
qc.ch(0, 1)   # CH
qc.swap(0, 1) # SWAP
qc.ccx(0,1,2) # Toffoli
qc.cp(θ,0,1)  # Controlled phase

Common Exam Questions

Q: What is the output state after applying H gate to |0⟩?

A: |+⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2

Q: How do you create a Bell state |Φ+⟩?

qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)

Q: What does qc.measure_all() do?

A: Adds measurement to ALL qubits, creates classical register automatically

Barriers and Identity

# Barrier - prevents optimization across it
qc.barrier()         # All qubits
qc.barrier(0, 1)     # Specific qubits

# Identity - does nothing (useful for timing)
qc.id(0)             # Identity on qubit 0
qc.delay(100, 0)     # Delay in dt units

Circuit Composition

# Compose circuits
qc1 = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc1.h(0)

qc2 = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc2.cx(0, 1)

# Append qc2 to qc1
qc1.compose(qc2, inplace=True)

# Or create new circuit
qc3 = qc1.compose(qc2)

# Reverse a circuit
qc_inverse = qc1.inverse()

⚠️ Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting that qubit indexing starts at 0
  • Confusing cx(control, target) order
  • Not understanding that measure_all() adds classical bits
keyTakeaways: Memorize common gate methods and their effects

lessons.title: Mock Exam 1: Circuit Basics
lessons.content:
📝 Mock Exam 1: Circuit Basics (20 Questions)

⏱️ Time: 30 minutes

This mock exam covers quantum circuit fundamentals. Try to complete it without looking at documentation.

Question 1

Which code correctly creates a quantum circuit with 3 qubits and 2 classical bits?

A) QuantumCircuit(3, 2)
B) QuantumCircuit(qubits=3, bits=2)
C) QuantumCircuit(2, 3)
D) QuantumCircuit.create(3, 2)

Question 2

What is the matrix representation of the Hadamard gate?

A) (1/√2)[[1, 1], [1, -1]]
B) [[1, 0], [0, -1]]
C) [[0, 1], [1, 0]]
D) [[1, 0], [0, 1]]

Question 3

qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.measure_all()

What are the possible measurement outcomes with equal probability?

A) 00 and 01
B) 00 and 11
C) 01 and 10
D) All four with equal probability

Question 4

Which method returns the depth of a quantum circuit?

A) qc.length()
B) qc.size()
C) qc.depth()
D) qc.num_gates()

Question 5

What is the effect of applying X gate followed by X gate?

A) Creates superposition
B) Returns to original state (identity)
C) Flips the phase
D) Creates entanglement

Question 6

In qc.cx(0, 1), which qubit is the control?

A) Qubit 1
B) Qubit 0
C) Both qubits
D) Neither qubit

Question 7

What does qc.barrier() do?

A) Adds a measurement
B) Prevents transpiler optimization across it
C) Resets qubits to |0⟩
D) Blocks all subsequent gates

Question 8

Which gate creates a phase of π/4 (T gate)?

A) qc.s(0)
B) qc.t(0)
C) qc.z(0)
D) qc.p(pi/4, 0)

Question 9

How do you get the inverse of a circuit?

A) qc.reverse()
B) qc.inverse()
C) qc.adjoint()
D) qc.dagger()

Question 10

What is qc.num_qubits for QuantumCircuit(5, 3)?

A) 3
B) 5
C) 8
D) 15

🎯 Answer Key

1. A - QuantumCircuit(3, 2)
2. A - Hadamard matrix
3. B - 00 and 11 (Bell state)
4. C - qc.depth()
5. B - XX = I (identity)
6. B - Qubit 0 is control
7. B - Prevents optimization
8. B and D - Both correct
9. B - qc.inverse()
10. B - 5 qubits
keyTakeaways: Bell state produces 00 and 11 with equal probability
depth() returns circuit depth, size() returns gate count
First argument of cx() is the control qubit

lessons.title: Operators & Quantum Info Review
lessons.content:
Operators & Quantum Information Review

📚 Key Exam Topic: ~20%

Understanding quantum states, operators, and the quantum_info module is essential for the certification.

Statevector

from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector
import numpy as np

# Create statevector from array
sv = Statevector([1, 0])  # |0⟩
sv = Statevector([0, 1])  # |1⟩
sv = Statevector([1/np.sqrt(2), 1/np.sqrt(2)])  # |+⟩

# From label
sv = Statevector.from_label('0')  # |0⟩
sv = Statevector.from_label('+')  # |+⟩
sv = Statevector.from_label('01') # |01⟩

# From circuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
sv = Statevector.from_instruction(qc)

# Key methods
print(sv.data)           # Get numpy array
print(sv.probabilities())# Measurement probabilities
print(sv.is_valid())     # Check normalization
print(sv.draw('latex'))  # Visualize

Operator Class

from qiskit.quantum_info import Operator

# From matrix
X = Operator([[0, 1], [1, 0]])
H = Operator([[1, 1], [1, -1]]) / np.sqrt(2)

# From circuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(1)
qc.h(0)
op = Operator(qc)

# Properties
print(op.data)           # Matrix
print(op.dim)            # Dimensions
print(op.is_unitary())   # Check unitarity

# Operations
op_composed = X @ H      # Matrix multiplication
op_tensor = X.tensor(H)  # Tensor product

SparsePauliOp

from qiskit.quantum_info import SparsePauliOp

# Create from list of (Pauli string, coefficient)
H = SparsePauliOp.from_list([
    ("ZZ", 1.0),
    ("XX", 0.5),
    ("YY", 0.5),
    ("II", -0.5)
])

# Properties
print(H.num_qubits)      # Number of qubits
print(H.coeffs)          # Coefficients
print(H.paulis)          # Pauli strings

# Used with Estimator for expectation values

Common Exam Questions

Q: How do you get measurement probabilities from a Statevector?

A: sv.probabilities()

Q: How do you check if an Operator is unitary?

A: op.is_unitary()

Q: What is the tensor product of |0⟩ and |1⟩?

A: |01⟩ - use sv1.tensor(sv2) or Statevector.from_label('01')

Fidelity & Metrics

from qiskit.quantum_info import state_fidelity, process_fidelity

# State fidelity
sv1 = Statevector.from_label('0')
sv2 = Statevector.from_label('+')
fid = state_fidelity(sv1, sv2)
print(f"Fidelity: {fid}")  # 0.5

# Process fidelity (between operators)
op1 = Operator.from_label('X')
op2 = Operator.from_label('X')
fid = process_fidelity(op1, op2)  # 1.0

lessons.title: Mock Exam 2: Operators & Execution
lessons.content:
📝 Mock Exam 2: Operators & Execution (20 Questions)

⏱️ Time: 30 minutes

This mock exam covers quantum operators, states, and circuit execution.

Question 1

Which creates a statevector for |+⟩ state?

A) Statevector.from_label('+')
B) Statevector([1, 1])
C) Statevector.plus()
D) Statevector('+')

Question 2

What does sv.probabilities() return for |+⟩?

A) [1, 0]
B) [0.5, 0.5]
C) [0.707, 0.707]
D) [0, 1]

Question 3

Which primitive computes expectation values?

A) Sampler
B) Estimator
C) Transpiler
D) Executor

Question 4

H = SparsePauliOp.from_list([("ZI", 1.0), ("IZ", 1.0)])

How many qubits does this operator act on?

A) 1
B) 2
C) 3
D) 4

Question 5

How do you run a circuit on AerSimulator?

A) AerSimulator.run(qc)
B) AerSimulator().run(qc)
C) qc.run(AerSimulator)
D) execute(qc, AerSimulator)

Question 6

What does Operator(qc).is_unitary() check?

A) If the circuit has measurements
B) If U†U = I
C) If the circuit is optimized
D) If all gates are real

Question 7

What is the default number of shots for Sampler?

A) 100
B) 1000
C) 1024
D) Infinite (exact)

Question 8

How do you get counts from a job result?

A) result.counts()
B) result.get_counts()
C) result.data.counts
D) result.measurements()

Question 9

What does state_fidelity(sv1, sv2) return for identical states?

A) 0
B) 0.5
C) 1
D) 2

Question 10

Which correctly creates a 2-qubit ZZ operator?

A) SparsePauliOp("ZZ")
B) SparsePauliOp.from_list([("ZZ", 1)])
C) Operator("ZZ")
D) PauliOp("ZZ")

🎯 Answer Key

1. A - Statevector.from_label('+')
2. B - [0.5, 0.5]
3. B - Estimator
4. B - 2 qubits
5. B - AerSimulator().run(qc)
6. B - Checks U†U = I
7. D - Default is exact simulation
8. B - result.get_counts()
9. C - Fidelity is 1
10. B - SparsePauliOp.from_list

lessons.title: Transpilation & Optimization Review
lessons.content:
Transpilation & Optimization Review

📚 Key Exam Topic: ~15%

Transpilation converts abstract circuits to hardware-executable form. Know the optimization levels and options!

Basic Transpilation

from qiskit import transpile, QuantumCircuit

qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)

# Basic transpilation
transpiled = transpile(qc)

# With options
transpiled = transpile(
    qc,
    basis_gates=['cx', 'id', 'rz', 'sx', 'x'],
    optimization_level=3,
    seed_transpiler=42
)

Optimization Levels

Level 0 No optimization

Just maps to basis gates

Level 1 Light optimization

Basic gate cancellation

Level 2 Medium optimization

Noise-aware routing (default for real hardware)

Level 3 Heavy optimization

Most aggressive, may take longer

Key Parameters

transpiled = transpile(
    qc,
    backend=backend,           # Target backend
    basis_gates=['cx', 'rz', 'sx'],  # Native gates
    coupling_map=[[0,1],[1,2]],      # Qubit connectivity
    initial_layout=[0, 2],           # Map logical to physical
    optimization_level=2,            # 0-3
    seed_transpiler=123              # For reproducibility
)

Common Exam Questions

Q: What happens if you don't specify a coupling_map?

A: Assumes all-to-all connectivity (no routing needed)

Q: What's the default optimization_level?

A: Level 1 (basic optimization)

Q: How do you see the final basis gates after transpilation?

transpiled.count_ops()

Coupling Maps

# Linear chain: 0-1-2-3
linear = [[0,1], [1,0], [1,2], [2,1], [2,3], [3,2]]

# From backend
from qiskit_ibm_runtime import QiskitRuntimeService
service = QiskitRuntimeService()
backend = service.backend('ibm_brisbane')
coupling = backend.coupling_map

⚠️ Exam Tips

  • Know the difference between optimization levels
  • Understand that SWAP gates are added for routing
  • Higher optimization = potentially longer compile time

lessons.title: Mock Exam 3: Full Practice (60 Questions)
lessons.content:
📝 Mock Exam 3: Full Practice Exam

⏱️ Time: 90 minutes | 60 Questions

This is a full-length practice exam simulating the real IBM certification. Complete without notes for the best practice.

Exam Structure

  • Questions 1-15: Quantum Circuits
  • Questions 16-30: Operators & States
  • Questions 31-40: Transpilation
  • Questions 41-50: Execution & Backends
  • Questions 51-60: Visualization & Tools

Sample Question 1 (Circuits)

qc = QuantumCircuit(3)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.cx(1, 2)

What state does this circuit create?

A) |000⟩ + |111⟩ (GHZ state)
B) |000⟩ + |100⟩
C) |000⟩ + |011⟩
D) W state

Sample Question 2 (Operators)

Which import is needed for SparsePauliOp?

A) from qiskit import SparsePauliOp
B) from qiskit.quantum_info import SparsePauliOp
C) from qiskit.primitives import SparsePauliOp
D) from qiskit.operators import SparsePauliOp

Sample Question 3 (Transpilation)

What is added to a circuit during transpilation when qubits are not directly connected?

A) Identity gates
B) SWAP gates
C) Barrier operations
D) Measurement operations

Sample Question 4 (Execution)

Which is NOT a valid way to create a backend instance?

A) AerSimulator()
B) service.backend('ibm_brisbane')
C) Backend('simulator')
D) service.least_busy()

Sample Question 5 (Visualization)

Which method draws a circuit as text output?

A) qc.draw()
B) qc.draw('text')
C) qc.print()
D) Both A and B

📋 Full Exam Access

The complete 60-question exam is available in the interactive practice mode. Click "Start Full Exam" to begin a timed session.

🎯 Sample Answers

1. A - GHZ state (|000⟩ + |111⟩)/√2
2. B - qiskit.quantum_info
3. B - SWAP gates for routing
4. C - Backend() is not valid
5. D - Both work for text
keyTakeaways: GHZ state created by H + cascade of CNOTs
SWAP gates enable operations between non-adjacent qubits

lessons.title: Final Review & Exam Tips
lessons.content:
Final Review & Exam Tips

🎓 You're Ready!

This final session provides key reminders and strategies for exam day success.

Quick Reference: Most Tested APIs

Circuit Methods

qc.h(0), qc.x(0), qc.cx(0,1)
qc.measure(0, 0), qc.measure_all()
qc.depth(), qc.size(), qc.num_qubits
qc.compose(), qc.inverse(), qc.copy()
qc.draw(), qc.barrier()

State & Operator Methods

Statevector.from_label('0')
Statevector.from_instruction(qc)
sv.probabilities(), sv.is_valid()
Operator(qc).is_unitary()
SparsePauliOp.from_list([...])

Execution Methods

transpile(qc, optimization_level=2)
Sampler().run(qc), Estimator().run(qc, obs)
AerSimulator().run(qc)
result.get_counts()

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Wrong: qc.cx(target, control)

Right: qc.cx(control, target)

Wrong: QuantumCircuit(clbits, qubits)

Right: QuantumCircuit(qubits, clbits)

Wrong: Forgetting to import from qiskit.quantum_info

Right: Know which module contains each class

Exam Day Strategy

⏱️

Time Management

~1.5 minutes per question. Flag difficult ones and return.

🔍

Read Carefully

Watch for "NOT", "EXCEPT", "ALL of the following"

🎯

Eliminate Wrong Answers

Often 2 answers are obviously wrong

💻

Code Reading

Trace through code mentally, step by step

Final Checklist

  • ☐ Know all single-qubit and common 2-qubit gates
  • ☐ Understand Bell state creation and measurement
  • ☐ Know Statevector and Operator methods
  • ☐ Understand transpilation levels and options
  • ☐ Know difference between Sampler and Estimator
  • ☐ Practice circuit visualization methods

🎉 Good Luck!

You've completed the IBM Qiskit Developer Certification preparation course. Trust your preparation and you'll do great!
keyTakeaways: Know which module contains each class
